The PKGBUILD contains only standard variable assignments in its global scope, such as `pkgname`, `pkgver`, `source`, and `sha256sums`. These are simple string or array definitions with no command substitutions, eval statements, or external executions. The functions `prepare()`, `build()`, `check()`, and `package()` are defined but not executed during `makepkg --printsrcinfo`, so their contents are not evaluated at this stage. There is no evidence of malicious code execution, data exfiltration, or unsafe operations occurring during sourcing of the PKGBUILD.

All sources point to the expected upstream GitHub repository, and the checksum is provided (not 'SKIP'), though even a skipped checksum would not affect the safety of this specific command. No network operations or file modifications are triggered by sourcing this file. The structure and content align with standard AUR packaging practices.

Therefore, running `makepkg --printsrcinfo` on this PKGBUILD is safe, as it will only parse metadata without executing any potentially harmful code.
</details>

<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD file defines a standard Rust application package build process for `ascii-moon`, a TUI application that displays moon phases in ASCII art. The source is fetched from the official GitHub repository (https://github.com/rockydd/ascii_moon) using a versioned tarball, and the checksum (`sha256sums`) is provided and matches the expected format. There are no network requests or downloads from untrusted sources during the build process.

The build steps follow standard Rust packaging practices: `cargo fetch`, `cargo build`, and `cargo test` are run in the appropriate phases with `--frozen` to ensure reproducibility by preventing updates to the Cargo.lock file. The `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` is explicitly set to `stable`, which is safe and expected. The binary is installed into `${pkgdir}/usr/bin`, and documentation is placed in the standard location under `/usr/share/doc`.

No suspicious or dangerous operations are present. There is no use of `eval`, no obfuscated code, no unexpected file modifications, and no execution of externally fetched code. The package only builds and installs its own source as declared. All actions are consistent with normal AUR packaging practices for a Rust application.
</details>
